utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Registrar, could you call the case number, please.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good day, Mr. President. Case number IT-04-74-T, the Prosecutor versus Prlic et al.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. Registrar. I would like to greet everyone present and I will now immediately give the floor to the registrar for IC numbers.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Several parties have submitted lists of documents to be tendered through Witness DD. The list submitted by the OTP shall be given Exhibit number IC 439. The list submitted by 1D shall be given Exhibit number IC 440. The list ship submitted by 2D shall be given Exhibit number IC 441, and the list submitted by 5D shall be given Exhibit number IC 442. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. There is an oral decision I would like to read out which grants the request for an extension of time limit. On the 21st of February, 2007, the Chamber was provided with two motions requesting extension of the time limit provided for in Rule 126 bis in the Rules of Procedure and Evidence. The motion concerned filing requests -- filing responses to a number motions that are pending before the Chamber. The Prosecution has requested an extension of the time limit to respond to the Defence motion that concerns the various forms of responsibility alleged in the indictment. The motion was filed on the 12th of February, 2007. The Trial Chamber hereby grants this request, and the time limit shall be extended until the 7th of March, 2007. The Defence requested an extension of time limit in order to respond to three Prosecution motions. The two motions that concern the Jablanica municipality filed on the 15th of February, 2007, and a motion that concerns Vares municipality filed on the 19th of February, 2007. The Defence has requested an extension of the time limit to respond to these three motions and would like the time limit to be extended until the 19th of March, 2007. The Chamber hereby decides to partially grant this request and grants an extension of the time limit up until the 12th of March, 2007. The Prosecution has another hour and 10 minutes. It's now 2.20. The Prosecution has the floor for an hour and 10 minutes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PORYVAEV
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. PORYVAEV
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Mr. Hadrovic.

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA HADROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: MR. PORYVAEV
utterances.text: Let's continue our job. I must repeat and ask you again, just keep straight on my questions. Only in such a way could we cope with our job today. Try not to comment and elaborate your responses if it's not absolutely necessary. Mr. Hadrovic, yesterday, this is page 56, lines 2, 3 of the transcript, you testified that you had been arrested for the second time and again taken to Heliodrom. Please tell me, when did it happen? When were you arrested for the second time?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA HADROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was arrested for the second time in the hospital, because I was there in the neurology department. They came to get me that day. Selentrovic [phoen] saw me and he wanted to take me away on that day. He didn't because and Dr. Begic wouldn't let him. In the evening Miro Kolobara and another young man arrived, and that evening at 11.30 they took me to the Heliodrom.

utterances.speaker: MR. PORYVAEV
utterances.text: What date? The date, please.

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA HADROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was in June, on the 25th or the 26th. I don't know the exact date, but that's the approximate date. I have a medical certificate that in fact states when I was taken away. I do have this certificate on me because later on I obtained it before I was to come here to the Tribunal.

utterances.speaker: MR. PORYVAEV
utterances.text: And were you placed in Heliodrom in some common hole with other detainees?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA HADROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I wasn't. At that time I was taken to solitary confinement in the Heliodrom complex. I was beaten up there and I remained in that cell for a hundred and -- days. I spent 147 days plus the other days. That would amount to about 160 days in solitary confinement at the Heliodrom. When they took me to the Heliodrom that evening, Kolobara from the Convicts Battalion waited for me -- Miro Marijanovic waited for me and Jako [phoen] Tomic, Ante Buhovac, and others.

utterances.speaker: MR. PORYVAEV
utterances.text: You have already mentioned these names, Buhovac, Marjanovic. What kind of uniform were they wearing? Do you remember?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA HADROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. They had uniforms with these white belts on them. I think this was the military police central prison. It was under the control of the military police.

utterances.speaker: MR. PORYVAEV
utterances.text: Did they have any insignia of the military police on their sleeves or somewhere else?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA HADROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, the HVO police.

utterances.speaker: MR. PORYVAEV
utterances.text: Did you know these people - I mean Marjanovic and Ante Buhovac - before?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA HADROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I knew them well. I knew many of those who were down there. I knew them because we spent the first few days together in the joint police complex that acted against the aggressor, but unfortunately later on there were differences based on uniforms and nationalities.

utterances.speaker: MR. PORYVAEV
utterances.text: How many solitary cells were there in the Heliodrom complex? Did you see it? Could you tell us now?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA HADROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I saw that very well, too, and I saw all of them, because I had to clean the corridors as ordered. In the part that I was in, there was a large metal door. In one part there were four. You then go through another passage and there were another four isolation cells there, and on the other side there were also four isolation cells and there was a large room and a kitchen in another area. But I could never gain access to the kitchen because they brought food to our cells.

utterances.speaker: MR. PORYVAEV
utterances.text: Were you alone in a solitary cell from the very beginning? And how long, if you were?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA HADROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: When they took me down that day after I had been beaten up badly, I spent a lot of time in that solitary confinement cell. Cibo was next to my cell. He worked for a certain water supply company and there were other prisoners near me, Zilic. Then there was Mirsad Mahmutcehajic. There was Vlado Fink and others. I could tell you all of their names and tell you which cells they were in, but later they kept 12 of us in one cell, and we had to relieve ourselves in a biscuit tin.

utterances.speaker: MR. PORYVAEV
utterances.text: I will ask you about conditions in the solitary cells a little bit later. But now I would like witness to be shown Exhibit P 05077. Please open your binder on the relevant number. Page 2 will be in the original language. Did you find the document?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA HADROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I found the document.

utterances.speaker: MR. PORYVAEV
utterances.text: This is a list -- for the record, this is a list of detainees detained in solitary cells of Heliodrom, with stamp and letterhead office for change of prisoners and other persons. Witness, just leaf through -- leaf down this list and try to recall if you remember all the people who are indicated there.

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA HADROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honours, I can confirm and guarantee that all these people live with me to this very day. I still see them, and I know each and every run of them. Unfortunately, some are abroad, but I know Zilic. His father is in the country, but his son is abroad. I couldn't say that there's a single person that I don't know. I know each and every one of them, from the first one to the last one. There are just two foreigners missing in this list, and I did testify that they were there. One was from Malaysia and the other one was from Germany.

utterances.speaker: MR. PORYVAEV
utterances.text: Okay. Just a moment. We see here 29 persons. Does it correspond to the reality that there were 29 persons, detainees, kept in the solitary cells?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA HADROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honours, in this list you just have a part that concerns those in solitary confinement. That was the area we were in. Then there was another part. I don't know anything about those individuals, but I know certain individuals who were in the large room. That's not a solitary confinement so I couldn't say it is, but there were three solitary confinement cells. There was a cell beneath the stairs and another one next to it, but in the big one where people from Roradorca [phoen] and Jasenica were -- they were there with their children. I knew some of them. I would sometimes see Katica and Jusuf. I knew them because they had a house in Donja Mahala and I would see them when I emptied the biscuit tin. And the ones I can see here were in my area. That's when you enter the solitary confinement cell to the right.

utterances.speaker: MR. PORYVAEV
utterances.text: Mr. Hadrovic, my question is, could you explain at least to yourself and to the Trial Chamber now what is your understanding why personally you were kept in the solitary cell?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA HADROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honours, I'm not going to lie. I have no reason to lie. I was taken to the solitary confinement cell for many reasons. Partly because I wouldn't allow certain things to happen, concern members of the HVO supported me in this. Concerned theft, the maltreatment of Serbs, et cetera. I didn't want to offend anyone because he had stayed with us. Your Honours, I can prove that for certain. The Serbs who are still alive to this very day and I can prove that I didn't want to maltreat anybody, the Bosniaks or the Croats.

utterances.speaker: MR. PORYVAEV
utterances.text: My question is now about the condition in the solitary cells, I mean the quality of good water, other facilities.

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA HADROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honours, let me tell you how much time I spent in the solitary confinement cell. During that period of time when I left the cell, I had lost 47 kilos. The conditions were non-existent. I can provide you with just one example. In the morning we received tea. We were given tea, but certain people gave us tin cups, but instead of putting sugar in the cups they would put salt in them. The food was there when the Red Cross came and brought it, but whatever remained, well, all of the detainees at the Heliodrom can tell you that they took this away and they didn't allow us to eat. And as far as the sleeping conditions are concerned, I had one blanket and that's all. I relieved myself in a biscuit tin, and I would receive one litre of water per day. So imagine what the conditions were like. I won't prove this myself. The entire town, all those who were there, will prove this.

utterances.speaker: MR. PORYVAEV
utterances.text: My next question -- thank you very much. My next question is did you perform any kind of job while you were -- while you were detained in this solitary cell?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA HADROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honours. Every morning I had to clean. I had to clean the toilets. I had to wash my dirty clothes without soap because they wouldn't provide me with any soap, and I had to clean the corridors. And there was all sorts of dirt. I can prove this.

utterances.speaker: MR. PORYVAEV
utterances.text: You just told that once you were brought to Heliodrom you were immediately beaten. I would like to clarify: By whom? I need the names of people to beat you up at the time.

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA HADROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: When I was taken there.

utterances.speaker: MR. PORYVAEV
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA HADROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The notorious Miro Kolobara. In Mostar there are two Miro Kolobaras. I apologise to one of them, the one who works in the post office. And the other one is hiding in Siroki Brijeg. He beat me up so badly. And Daka Tomic, Ante Buhovac, and Miro Marijanovic. And believe it or not they beat me so badly and then tied one of my arms to the bed, and I know that I woke up covered in blood. I found a piece of mirror, and when I saw myself, well, I was covered in blood all over. You can see the results on my head, my jaw, my nose. You can see the scars. Doctors in Mostar and throughout the world, wherever I had --

utterances.speaker: MR. PORYVAEV
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA HADROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: -- can also prove this.

utterances.speaker: MR. PORYVAEV
utterances.text: Did you see anyone else from your inmates being beaten, or did you have any knowledge about that?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA HADROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honours. I saw a lot of things down there. I had occasion to see how they were beating up a policeman, and I also saw an action that was carried out. This is what a young man told me who was in a cell with me later on. This was in July at Ortijes. They captured five young men. One of them was Golos. And the leader of that group was so badly beaten -- he was beaten to death. He lied -- his corpse lied in the cell for three days. I cleaned the cells. I can prove this together with all these people who are listed here, believe me. He died. They took him away.

utterances.speaker: MR. PORYVAEV
utterances.text: Thank you very much. And you just mentioned Kolobara and other persons. Did any HVO soldiers or other persons who were not the Heliodrom guards have access to these solitary cells?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA HADROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I won't avoid this subject. Juka [phoen] was the first one to have access to the solitary confinement cells. And then all of Tuta's soldiers, especially if there had been victims on battlefields, they would maltreat the detainees, and they'd force us to sing various songs. They made us say certain terrible things when singing these songs.

utterances.speaker: MR. PORYVAEV
utterances.text: My next question: When were you registered by the Red Cross, if you were registered at all?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA HADROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. The Red Cross registered us later. There was -- Stanko Bozic issued an order. Ante Buhovac took us out, and below the building of the central prison, as they called it, there was a cinema hall, and across the road there was a canteen for the HVO.

utterances.speaker: MR. PORYVAEV
utterances.text: For what purposes were you taken there?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA HADROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: They took us there in fact so as to not report us to the Red Cross, but thanks to Humackic Hajro, well, he accidentally saw us quite by chance through the window, and he reported to Ms. Karolina, who was responsible for the Red Cross at the time. And on the 18th -- on the 16th of August, I don't know the exact date -- I have the card in fact that shows when I was registered. I don't know the exact date. It was on the 16th or the 18th, give or take a few days. Then we were seen by chance. They reported that they were hiding us, and she found us, and that's when we were registered. I have that certificate from the Red Cross, so I was able to go on be provided with medical treatment wherever I wanted to go. And then in Sarajevo it was possible for me to have treatment because I had lost a lot of weight.

utterances.speaker: MR. PORYVAEV
utterances.text: Mr. Hadrovic, you just mentioned Humackic Hajro. Was he an inmate as well?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA HADROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. He was a killed workman. He had some sort of work down there. I thanked him, and I'm still grateful to him because perhaps he saved my life. I know that many who were in solitary confinement cells never returned to prison, to the solitary confinement cells or to the town of Mostar.

utterances.speaker: MR. PORYVAEV
utterances.text: Then my next question is: When you saw ICRC person for the first time did they enter the solitary cells?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA HADROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, they entered the solitary confinement cells because they couldn't drive us out at the time. They couldn't take us out because these people arrived before we were supposed to go to that cinema hall. We'd sit there from the morning until 9.00 in the evening, until the Red Cross left. It all depended on the time they would actually spend there.

utterances.speaker: MR. PORYVAEV
utterances.text: My question is: Were you taken to the cinema hall on several occasions or only ones?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA HADROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: They took us there on a number of occasions because the Red Cross came on a number of occasions since people reported to them. I can mention the people or mention the names of the people who reported to the Red Cross. They're still in Mostar. There's Jovanka Hevdjija [phoen], Zenic Sisic [phoen], Jadranko Jelenko [phoen], Vajdjak [phoen], a professor who has now returned, and there are many who can now confirm this. They are witnesses in Mostar. They can confirm certain things so that the entire world can know what happened down there and can know about the abuse that took place there.

utterances.speaker: MR. PORYVAEV
utterances.text: Thank you very much. I would like Witness to be shown Exhibit P 04352.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Just a minute, before we move on to another document. Witness, I regret the fact that I have to intervene, but there are certain inevitable questions I have to put to you. There is a list consisting of 29 detainees that were kept in solitary confinement. This list has been signed by Mr. Pusic, who is apparently the person present here in the courtroom. Mr. Pusic was in an office for the exchange of prisoners and other persons. The list was established in September, on the 15th of September, in fact. As far as you know, were there any people in this list who were exchanged?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] To be quite frank, Your Honour, I'm looking at the names. Some did leave the solitary confinement cells earlier, but I don't know whether they were exchanged, but some did leave early year. Paruk Pirolic [phoen].

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. I'll move on to another subject. A minute ago you said that there were people in solitary confinement cells that were no longer seen. They went missing in a certain sense. Among these 29 detainees are there any individuals who disappeared without a trace?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, the person that was killed isn't here, and I don't know anything about him. I asked about it and everything. But of these people here, I just know that one has disappeared. As to the others, some of them left up there, and they were up there --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Which is the person who disappeared and is on this list?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] There's a young man that's missing here, and they were -- he was taken out of the station, and I had to clean the station myself, and all the others --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] But my question is: Of the names on the list, which have disappeared?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] These people all stayed, but some of them were taken out of the station before their time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Mr. Poryvaev.

utterances.speaker: MR. PORYVAEV
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. PORYVAEV
utterances.text: So I would like you to open up P 04352. Find, please, this number. It must be the first document in the bundle.

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA HADROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: 4352, is that what it is?

utterances.speaker: MR. PORYVAEV
utterances.text: Have you found it? Yes. This, just for the record --

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA HADROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I have.

utterances.speaker: MR. PORYVAEV
utterances.text: This is a document which was submitted to Mr. Bruno Stojic by SIS warden Stanko Bozic, dated on the 20th of August, 1993. Mr. Hadrovic, I would like you to turn to page 1 of the document to items, 1, 2, 3. Dealing with quantity of -- yes. Did you find it?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA HADROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PORYVAEV
utterances.text: Could you tell me if the contents of the document that the quality and quantity of food needed to be improved and the conditions in solitary cells were bad corresponds to the reality you just witnessed while being detained in the solitary cell?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA HADROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honour, that's how it was for us down there. I'd rather sleep with an animal than sleep down there where I slept because the conditions were terrible. There was the sewer that was dripping with water, so you can imagine what that was like with the sewer system like that dripping into the cells.

utterances.speaker: MR. PORYVAEV
utterances.text: So --

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA HADROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Conditions were at zero.

utterances.speaker: MR. PORYVAEV
utterances.text: Okay. Okay. My next question is: Did you see while being detained in the solitary cell any high-ranking HVO representatives who were not just the Heliodrom staff members?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA HADROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I did, Your Honour. When we were in the cinema hall I saw Mr. Praljak walking towards the canteen down there.

utterances.speaker: MR. PORYVAEV
utterances.text: Which Praljak?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA HADROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Slobodan Praljak.

utterances.speaker: MR. PORYVAEV
utterances.text: Witness, you're not answering my question. My question was if they visited you in the solitary cells. Not personally you but other inmates as well. I mean, inspected solitary cells. We'll talk about Slobodan Praljak a little bit later if it's necessary. Did you understand my question?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA HADROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I did understand it, and I'll answer it now. On one occasion doctors came by, and among the doctors was Mr. Pohara. He wanted to write something for someone so that they could be released. Sejo Pasic came with him, and he saw me. As I saw Pohara when he was with the president once, Mr. Alija Izetbegovic, I asked him what party it was that he was in -- or, rather, that I was in and I said that I wasn't interested in any party. All I was interested in was to be set free and for the town to be pure and clean and liberated, and I wasn't interested in any party. And I'm not interested in any parties now either.

utterances.speaker: MR. PORYVAEV
utterances.text: And what was his response?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA HADROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: His response was quite simple. He says, "You can't do anything. You can't go anywhere because you're not a member of any party." And that's where I stayed till the last day.

utterances.speaker: MR. PORYVAEV
utterances.text: You mentioned person Sejo Pasic. What was he? What was his position at that time?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA HADROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was like this: Sejo Pasic, or Sead Pasic, and all of his people were the Croatian Defence Council. I don't know what ranks they held. And while I was in the hospital once, I saw him but I didn't dare say hello to him because I was afraid that he might kill me. All I know is that he's no kind of decent man, not today either.

utterances.speaker: MR. PORYVAEV
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you very much. And were you moved from the solitary cells after being discovered by the Red Cross? I mean when. Did you stay there for some period of time long or not?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA HADROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honour, although the Red Cross found us, I stayed on as did many of the others on the list except for perhaps seven or eight persons. We stayed to the very end. I left solitary confinement just before Christmas. I was in there up until then, and I will give you all the names and surnames. Placo Saric [phoen], Ledje Mehic [phoen], Jusuf Katica, Rudi Pilot was taken. Rado Pink [phoen] was taken away. He was taken to Ljubuski. Mirso Mahmutcehajic was taken to Ljubuski. So was Zilic, he was taken to Ljubuski. And there were just 12 of us left down there. And in the other two cells there was also -- there were the two Demirovic brothers, Semir, and Suka [phoen], nicknamed Coric, an active-duty policeman.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'm going to get to the heart of the matter. Now, the document that you have before you by comes from Mr. Stanko Bozic addressed to Mr. Bruno Stojic is a document which was written following the visit by Mr. Franko Fara [phoen] from the Red Cross, and this document highlights three problems: Detainees working, the quality and quantity of the food, and the bad conditions in solitary confinement cells. Now, when we read this document, this letter, we see that the author of it is concerned because he doesn't wish to find himself accountable to a Tribunal one day, and he says that there are a number of people who had been killed and wounded and that this number seems to be on the increase. And there is certainly a reference to the people who were sent outside the prison to do work. Now, what can you tell us about this paragraph? And that's much more interesting than the details that you quoted a moment ago. Could you tell us? The author of this article, what situation is he referring to when he speaks of people killed and wounded at work, at the workplace?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I'll repeat what I said a moment ago. The conditions were terrible. People went to work, went out to do work. And probably when Stanko Bozic signed this saying that people weren't going out to do work then I believe that the gentleman had in mind those who had been ill or had been beaten. But otherwise, people went out to work on a regular basis, and I can guarantee that with my life. Because there were shaves -- there were shovels and picks and other things used when the people went out to work. They were filed up in the hall. And I know the three brothers.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Did they work inside the prison or outside?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] They worked up at the front lines building bunkers and carrying sacks in Santica Street.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Poryvaev, carry on with your work.

utterances.speaker: MR. PORYVAEV
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you very much. I will continue with this question.

utterances.speaker: MR. PORYVAEV
utterances.text: Witness, do you remember any names of people, detainees who were killed or wounded while they were performing forced labour?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA HADROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Miro Copil. He was the first. I can prove that straight away. The man is still ill and sick. He's in the police. He still has operations to undergo after that wounding. And then I can tell you also there was Damir Huskovic. I saw him from the station. He had been beaten up, but he wasn't wounded. He was beaten up because he didn't want to carry the sacks in Santic Street. He saw his friends, and they ought to lose their heads because all the buildings there were razed to the ground.

utterances.speaker: MR. PORYVAEV
utterances.text: But any people killed? Do you remember their names? You just mentioned two brothers. Do you remember their names?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA HADROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honour, it was a long time ago. I just can't seem to remember their names, although I know that they were killed up at the front line. That I know for certain. They were people from Sovici. And many disappeared from up there, never to return. And I can confirm that, Your Honour, because that same case is being dealt with in the town of Mostar. Many people took money for giving false testimony.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I have to ask you a question, because a few days ago there was a witness who said that at Stotina, near Donja Mahala, there were people who came from Heliodrom to do work there. Now, to your knowledge were there prisoners from Heliodrom who did forced labour at Stotina?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, what I'm going to tell you now is something that I will certainly never deny. That is the land of my forefathers, and it was confiscated during Tito's time. Now, from that place a sniper shot mostly at Donja Mahala, Luka, Sehovina and other places. I know the policeman I saw him with my very own eyes, and his name was Lozancic. They called him Suha Ruka, or thin hand. And I knew a young guy who sorted the holes on the building because I tended to my cows there and I know where the tanks were positioned. I know that very well because my nephew, he was there, too, so I can confirm this 100 per cent. It was from Stotina and from Visnjica that the -- the places were targeted, because I know a young guy who went to --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The detainees in Heliodrom, did they -- were they taken out to do forced labour at Stotina? I said "work." It says in the English text "forced labour." I said "work." In French I said "work"; I didn't speak of forced labour. So work, who were taken to do work there. To your knowledge, the detainees from Heliodrom, did they go to Stotina to work? It's a yes or a no.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Your Honour. They had to work.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Do you have a name or several names?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, I do. Ramiz Hodzic. He now lives in the western part of Mostar, and he personally did this work, and he openly said Mujo [phoen] Lozancic is killing innocent children. And I saw that same man, Lozancic, wearing a camouflage white uniform. And that was already in December. I can confirm that, because when I left the station I saw him personally wearing a camouflage, white camouflage uniform and a hat, and a sniper with optic sights.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] To summarise what you said in lines 14 and onwards, you said that Mr. Ramiz Hodzic told you that Miro Lozancic had killed innocent children. Is that what you said?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Your Honour, it is. That's exactly what he said.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Continue, Mr. Poryvaev.

utterances.speaker: MR. PORYVAEV
utterances.text: I would like Witness to be shown Exhibit P 07498.

utterances.speaker: MR. PORYVAEV
utterances.text: Please open the document bearing this number, 7498 for you. And this is the list of prisoners of war and civilians who died during work. Please look at the list and tell us if you come across any names that sound familiar to you.

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA HADROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Huso Ljevo, Mustafa Taso, Semir Cehajic, Enver Kajtas, Remzo Sabljic, Enver Puzic.

utterances.speaker: MR. PORYVAEV
utterances.text: Did you know all of them? I mean the ones you mentioned.

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA HADROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I did, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. PORYVAEV
utterances.text: And how do you know that they were killed?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA HADROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This was like this, quite frankly: I know when the people who went with them up to the front line or many of them who went to Vojna never returned to Heliodrom. That's what I heard from the same people who went and came back, but these others never returned, and many of them stayed in Vojna.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Sir, a question from me. This document is addressed to Mr. Berislav Pusic, and he was in charge of the prisoner exchange. Since these people are apparently dead, we don't see whether there could have been an exchange of any kind except to exchange bodies, corpses. So how can you interpret this, this list addressed to the prisoner exchange office? Do you have an explanation for that or not?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I'll have to apologise greatly later on precisely to this person, as far as this person is concerned, but it was more other people who asked about this and wondered rather than Berislav Pusic. Sagolj wondered more and so did the others as far as I saw it. Now, I'll tell you of a misunderstanding that came about later on. Now, this man here with his name and surname, well, I might even sort of in a way be grateful to him perhaps for something. I don't want -- or, rather, I want to be able to look everyone straight in the eyes, because tomorrow my child will have to live in that town, Mostar, with all of us together. So I don't want to inflict evil on anyone without cause. Other people can't look me in the eyes because they killed my people and issued orders for people to be incarcerated like me, and I became very ill as a result.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] A question from the Bench.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MINDUA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Witness, the document says that it is a list of prisoners of war and civilians who died during work. Now, you used the word "killed." Can you clarify that? Under what conditions did these people lose their lives?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, I can tell you, Your Honour. They carried sacks on their backs, many of them who passed by through many bunkers in Santic Street and that Bulevar there. It was burnt down to the ground and Santic Street too. Perhaps it was members of the BH army who shot. I can't say they didn't. But they had to, because the front line moved. The lines moved and each house in Santic Street was destroyed, because you couldn't advance that way and set up a front line. That's all I can say. You couldn't establish a line in any other, and that's how people were killed, lost their lives. Many of them lost their lives from the bullets and shells along that same front line.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] For the transcript, we can note that the last line says that the following persons died of natural causes, Esad Kolak and Mujo Boskailo who are not among the 37 others. Mr. Poryvaev, please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. PORYVAEV
utterances.text: Witness, when were you released from Heliodrom?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA HADROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honour, I was supposed to leave on the 19th of September, 1994. However, according to -- well, when they asked me which way I'd go after I left I said to the right, to Donja Mahala, and they said, "No you're not." And I said, "All right, fine." And I asked them the reason, and they said the right side belongs to the BH army. And I said that's the property of my forefathers, right by Vranica and the Krleze. You can go there. And I said, "No, I want to go to Donja Mahala. That's where my brothers are and cousins. I want to go there." So I left last, and this is something that can be confirmed, because everybody knows how I left. Everybody was there and looked and were able to see. Hamdija Jahic was there. He was the head. I was just about to board a vehicle but I was finally released on the 22nd --

utterances.speaker: MR. PORYVAEV
utterances.text: Mr. Hadrovic, just a moment. Please clarify the date. You mentioned 19th of -- September 19, 1994. Is that correct? Are you accurate about the date or your expected release?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA HADROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I expected to be released then because I wanted to go to a third country, but I wasn't given permission to do that. I just couldn't do that.

utterances.speaker: MR. PORYVAEV
utterances.text: When were you released?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA HADROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: On the 22nd of March, 1994. I was released last. Cehajic and the others, Hamdija Agic [phoen] and the others --

utterances.speaker: MR. PORYVAEV
utterances.text: One question remained unresolved, undiscussed from yesterday, because this part of my examination is already over, but have still a little bit of time and I will ask this question: Mr. Hadrovic, you were -- at some point you were guarding the Old Bridge. When were you released from Heliodrom, did you get any information, knowledge, what had happened to the Old Bridge?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA HADROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PORYVAEV
utterances.text: Please tell the Trial Chamber.

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA HADROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'll tell the Trial Chamber the truth, the real truth. I have a document and a photograph too. Mr. Praljak was with us in the old town at the time, and he said that -- Mr. Praljak, the general. General Praljak. And I took a photograph, because I wanted to be seen standing next to a general who had already started to --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreter didn't understand what.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And I took a photograph of him and Mr. Culajsic [phoen], Ali Pasalic [phoen], Hasic, and Kemo, the small pilot. Your Honour, then I took another photograph and I stood next to --

utterances.speaker: MR. PORYVAEV
utterances.text: Witness, it's not a responsive answer. I would ask you just to keep to the point.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: And what period are we speaking about?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Karnavas.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: And what period are we talking about?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] He didn't say he took a photograph with Mr. Prlic. So if somebody has to intervene, it is, I assume, Mr. Praljak's counsel, not Mr. Prlic's counsel.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: I beg to differ, Your Honour. I'm entitled to have a clear record, and if the witness is not giving a clear because the Prosecution is not listening to that information, I'm entitled to ask the question and intervene. It doesn't necessarily mean that I can only intervene for my client. And I would like to see any jurisprudence anywhere that says that.

utterances.speaker: MR. PORYVAEV
utterances.text: I'm asking you about the Old Bridge. What happened to the Old Bridge? The fate of the Old Bridge.

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA HADROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The Old Bridge, when I arrived, well that's what -- I was doing labour when the Old Bridge was destroyed. They humiliated me at Heliodrom --

utterances.speaker: MR. PORYVAEV
utterances.text: When?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA HADROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: -- I was left without a work post.

utterances.speaker: MR. PORYVAEV
utterances.text: When?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA HADROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was at Heliodrom --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Witness, we're having trouble following you because you're mixing up various things. You just mentioned a photograph with Mr. Praljak. Then you say you were humiliated at Heliodrom, then you go on to another subject. Try and focus and answer specifically to the question you've been asked. When I ask you the questions, you answer very well, so do the same for Mr. Poryvaev's questions. Otherwise we're all lost, and Mr. Karnavas will be getting up on his feet, and he did so to focus on this problem. So try and be as precise in your answers as possible. I'm sure that lots of things are going round your head, but the Prosecution is giving you a question line and try to stick that and answer Mr. Poryvaev's questions. Mr. Poryvaev ask your question again and they are geared towards providing information for us Judges.

utterances.speaker: MR. PORYVAEV
utterances.text: What happened to the Old Bridge and when?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA HADROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The bridge was destroyed.

utterances.speaker: MR. PORYVAEV
utterances.text: When?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA HADROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was at the Heliodrom at the time that the Old Bridge was destroyed.

utterances.speaker: MR. PORYVAEV
utterances.text: You don't know the date?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA HADROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was in September, October, or November. I don't know the exact date, because later I was provoked on account of the Old Bridge. I was frequently humiliated because I had been on the Old Bridge.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Kovacic.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, there are two matters. We have a time problem or problem as far as the description of time periods are concerned, because the witness has already said that he guarded bridges in Mostar in 1992. But now that we're dealing with this issue the witness quite clearly stated at the time the Old Bridge was destroyed I was at the Heliodrom. So we're now dealing with hearsay or -- or what? Hearsay certainly isn't appropriate in this case.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Poryvaev, apparently when the Old Bridge was destroyed he was at the Heliodrom. So perhaps it is not really useful to ask questions about the destruction of the Old Bridge since we have had witnesses who were present when the Old Bridge actually collapsed. So let's not waste any more time.

utterances.speaker: MR. PORYVAEV
utterances.text: Yes. Only one final question.

utterances.speaker: MR. PORYVAEV
utterances.text: Did you get any information who destroyed the bridge, the Old Bridge?

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours -- just a minute, Witness, please. That is what is at issue. If we are going to admit hearsay another 5.000 people from Mostar can be called here and asked about what is being said in the town of Mostar. We can provide articles about this, too, but that's besides the point.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Mr. Kovacic, but you know that hearsay isn't excluded according to the case law of this Tribunal. So you were at the Heliodrom. Was the destruction of the Old Bridge mention, and what were you told with this regard?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] When the Old Bridge collapsed, everyone said way know that tanks went to Stotina, and they opened fire behind the prison itself, but the detainees who went up there to construct bunkers on Stotina said the Old Bridge has been destroyed. Barakovic and another gentleman have destroyed the Old Bridge, the symbol of Mostar. I can't remember the exact date because I was in solitary confinement. So just imagine how sick I was.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Witness, what you have said about the Old Bridge has no interest in relation to the fact that you were at the Heliodrom. But there is something that you have said that has aroused my curiosity. You said that there were tanks apparently at the Heliodrom and they opened fire from the Heliodrom. Have I misunderstood your testimony?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, Your Honours, you have understood me correctly. There were tanks at the Heliodrom, around the hangars.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, stop there. Did you yourself see the tanks around the Heliodrom and the hangars?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Your Honours. I did see them with my very own eyes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. My second question. You said you heard them open fire. Did you hear the shots being fired?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, we did, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Now, the third question: What did they open fire on?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, all I can say is this: I was told by my colleagues that they opened fire on civilians on the Old Bridge and on Blagaj, on Semovac, and on Stotina. They opened fire everywhere in Donja Mahala. That's where they fired from, because when the armija started advancing everything would be blown up around the barracks itself where we were kept in confinement.

utterances.speaker: MR. PORYVAEV
utterances.text: Who opened the fire?

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Kovacic, you'll cross-examine the witness about this.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] But just one comment if I may. We don't really intend to cross-examine this witness. This witness has no value for us. But since you put this question, I believe that for the 100th time the witness didn't understand you. When he mentions the opening fire, I understand his Bosnian language. He's not talking about specific tanks that were apparently at the Heliodrom. His answers are not answers to your questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. It seems that there may be a linguistic problem here. I believe that you said that there were tanks at the Heliodrom.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Your Honours, there were tanks at the Heliodrom.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] What do you consider to be a tank?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, a tank has caterpillar tracks. I served in Tito's army. I know what a tank is. I was a tank crewman. I know what a tank is.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. So you are saying under oath that there were tanks at the Heliodrom.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, that's what I'm claiming.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: I would like to -- to follow up a bit of this. Did you ever notice that such tanks fired shots from the area near the Heliodrom?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, when I went out of my solitary confinement cell I saw with my very own eyes. I was in the dormitories where others were, and I looked in the direction of the hangar. I know by heart where they were positioned and what direction they opened fire in. I know the positions where ABiH had members in Podvelezje were. They opened fire on these positions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] My colleague is very precise, just as I am, but what we want to know is the following -- all my colleagues want to know the following: Did you see the tanks fire? Did you see a shell coming out of the barrel? Did you see the shell coming out of the barrels of the tanks, and did you see the barrel smoking? Did you hear and see this? It's a very precise question.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Your Honours. I saw this with my very own eyes because it was a distance of 20 to 30 metres. That's where the tanks were positioned. They were behind the hangars and that's the position from which they opened fire. Your Honours, I'm not lying. I saw this with my very own eyes. I saw these tanks, and I saw the tanks heading off in the direction of Varda. When I went out of the solitary confinement cell later, when I went to empty the can that we relieved ourselves in, I could see all this.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] If you saw it others must have seen it too. You couldn't have been the only person who saw these tanks at the Heliodrom.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, naturally I wasn't the only person to have seen that. All of those up there in the dormitories saw that. The two floors and the attic. Everyone saw that, not just me. In that central prison, there weren't just 4 or 500 of us. There were over 2.000 of us. People slept in the corridors and everywhere.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I don't see the word in English that I heard in French. Perhaps the B/C/S has been translated directly into French. In French it says, "everyone saw the spectacle." In English it says, "We saw that." Did you use the word "spectacle" in your own language?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, let me say the following, Your Honours: I did, because everyone saw those tanks setting off in the direction of the town. They saw where they opened fire from. And in -- and, yes, there was a great spectacle when the Old Bridge was destroyed. I was one of the main persons at the Old Bridge, and I was humiliated and remained without a job. I can prove this for certain.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Let me -- let me continue with a series of questions. We have two things now in the air. I asked you whether you had seen tanks fire, shoot, from the vicinity of the Heliodrom and you said, "Yes." So did you see what these tanks were shooting at from Heliodrom, what they were aiming at?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The tank positioned right by the prison that opened fire in the direction of Blagaj and Dracevice where the old Austrian tower was the armija was there and that's the direction they fired in. I saw this with my very own eyes. I saw them opening fire and hitting the white stone that that tower is built of. To this very day you can still see the traces of impact. You can see holes. But I didn't see them opening fire on the Old Bridge. All I know is that those who were on Stotina, those who were digging trenches, they said that they were building fortifications of some kind for tanks. That's what I saw.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Thank you. And you then said you saw tanks move. I suppose that they moved in a northern direction, in the direction of Mostar; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: And how many tanks did you see move? Was it one, two, five?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Some were behind the hangar. Others were in the direction of Varda. One was on Hum. I know about the one on Hum. It was hit for sure. And I know about two other tanks. People told me about them. And I saw them moving through the barracks in the direction of the town. They were most likely going towards Stotina because that's the information I was provided with, and that's the location from which they opened fire on the Old Bridge.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Thank you. If I might just go on with another question, Mr. Karnavas, before you intervene. You have indicated but not very clearly that you were aware of the moment when the Old Bridge was hit. First, I'm not sure whether I understood you correctly and, if it is so, could you describe what made you think that the Old Bridge at that moment had been successfully targeted?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, it's difficult for me to say this but I'll have to. I'd been maltreated so badly, humiliated, when they destroyed the Old Bridge, and I remained without a job. That's when I was extremely humiliated. And, Your Honours, what I've said, I've already said that about Mostar, where the same sort of conflicts are ongoing. I have no reason to lie. All I can say is the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: That is understood. That is understood, and we have all the understanding also for the traumatic effect the destruction of the Old Bridge may have had on many inhabitants from -- and people from Mostar. My question was a different one. I asked you whether the moment the bridge was hit and destroyed whether you -- you had some perception of this in Heliodrom, whether there was a special noise, or whether you are just telling us what you have heard others tell you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] To be precise in one word, on the day that the Old Bridge was destroyed, was this information provided to everyone at the Heliodrom, and what did the detainees tell each other about this? It's very clear.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, I'll answer that question precisely. When the Old Bridge was destroyed all the detainees were sad. I, too, because it was difficult for me.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Before you felt sad -- just a minute. My colleague will take the floor to put another question to you. But before they felt sad, it was necessary to be provided with information. So were you provided with the information?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, yes. Members of the HVO, the policemen who were on guard at the time it, informed us of the fact. They informed us.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. I apologise to my colleague, who has a question for you now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: We are all of a lively temperament. So I take it now from your last answer that there was nothing which would indicate to you at the moment when the bridge fell that now the bridge falls, this sound only means the bridge falls, but you only learned about it because people from the HVO and later on inmates who had been out for work told you so; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Your Honours, that's correct. But there was shooting too.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Thank you. I apologise. Your patience has been tried. Mr. Karnavas, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Thank you. Your Honour, I just -- with the utmost of respect, on page 30, line 6 to 8 you asked the gentleman in which direction the tanks went, and then you went on a step further and indicated, "I suppose they moved in a northern direction, in the direction of Mostar; is that correct?" Now --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: That was a leading question. I should not have asked that.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Well, it wasn't so much it was leading because obviously Judges can ask leading questions at times, I would say, just as lawyers on cross-examination can do so, but I believe when -- by suggesting -- by saying, "I suppose they moved," it causes some concern, especially when the supposition is being given to the witness itself. So I just want to ask kindly that perhaps in the future we could avoid these sorts of questions that might suggest an answer to a witness who seems overly malleable. I'm not saying that that was the intent, but I'm saying that he is rather malleable in our respective, you know, and collective opinion.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: I take your point.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. Counsel has raised an issue, but if the question was put by a Judge it means there was a reason, a certain logic. As a rule, when Judges put questions there is a certain logic. When you mentioned the tanks that were there, we believe that we -- you wanted to say that there were tanks that were moving, and my colleague and I would have said the same thing. If they were moving, they moved in a certain direction. Did you in fact say that as far as you know there were tanks that left the Heliodrom and set off in a certain direction?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, naturally. They can't go down towards the aluminium institute. They went to the town. Naturally he know the points of the compass. I wasn't that naive.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] So you in fact said they moved. The Judges didn't suggest this to you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And given the fact that they had moved, well, they could have moved any number of directions, north, south, east, west. As far as you were concerned, which direction did they set off in? There are four possibilities.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, there are quite a few possibilities, quite a few directions the tanks could set off in.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] But in your opinion.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, in my opinion they set off in the direction of the north, the town, the bridge, Stotina.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. So we haven't suggested anything. The witness was following his own reasoning.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Poryvaev, how much time do you still have? Mr. Registrar. I know the Judges have taken up some time but we're dealing with certain essential matters and this can't be avoided. Mr. Poryvaev, how much time do you need to conclude your examination-in-chief?

utterances.speaker: MR. PORYVAEV
utterances.text: Just I think not much more than 10 minutes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Your Honour, I would ask for an accounting. I would ask for an accounting. The gentleman was given one hour and 10 minutes. If we are going to be held strictly, so should be the Prosecutor.

utterances.speaker: MR. PORYVAEV
utterances.text: What accounting is it of yours, Mr. Karnavas? It is the registry.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: That's what I'm asking for, an accounting of the time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Poryvaev, you have used up an hour and 27 minutes. We gave you two hours, but you don't have to use up two full hours, especially if the questions are put by the Judges that dealt with the issues that you were dealing with. You said that you needed another 10 minutes. Try to conclude within those 10 minutes. We will then have a break and we will let the Defence cross-examine the witness. So please continue with your examination-in-chief for another 10 minutes. And the Judges will not intervene.

utterances.speaker: MR. PORYVAEV
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. PORYVAEV
utterances.text: Mr. Hadrovic, you mentioned today that at some point you saw Mr. Slobodan Praljak in Heliodrom in the canteen area. My question is: From what premises did you see him?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA HADROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I saw him from the cinema hall, which is below the central prison. Across the road opposite there was the officers' mess. I saw him with my very own eyes. I knew him in the town of Mostar too. I also have photographs of him together with myself, and I admired him for the fight against our joint enemy. I can prove this. I have the relevant documents and photographs. If necessary, I can show them to Their Honours. Mr. Praljak knows with whom he had his photograph taken and where this was done.

utterances.speaker: MR. PORYVAEV
utterances.text: Thank you very much. And when were these photos taken?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA HADROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The photographs were taken before the conflict, on the Old Bridge. I couldn't find them then, but I have found them now and I have them now. I have them on me.

utterances.speaker: MR. PORYVAEV
utterances.text: And which -- and which year? Before the conflict? It might be 10 years ago, before the conflict, or more or less?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA HADROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: You're quite right to say that. Those photographs were taken when the Neretva was crossed. That was in June or July. We were sitting and the photographs were taken. Mr. Praljak was there, Mr. Arif Pasalic, Ica Lasic [phoen], Kemal, Pilot, and Hasic Pilot. And I was with him on the other photograph. And I was full of admiration when he said we will drive the enemy away. He won't leave any traces, but unfortunately that is not what happened.

utterances.speaker: MR. PORYVAEV
utterances.text: What do you mean July and June? What year?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA HADROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was in June after the Neretva had been crossed. The Neretva was crossed on the 11th or 12th.

utterances.speaker: MR. PORYVAEV
utterances.text: Yes, I understand you. I understand you. Year?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA HADROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Which year? In 1992 and 1993.

utterances.speaker: MR. PORYVAEV
utterances.text: 1990 -- no, photos taken what year?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Just a minute. I said I wouldn't put any questions. You took the same photograph in two different years? Either it's in 1992 or 1993.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The photographs that were taken. They were taken in 1993, just before -- or immediately prior to the conflict. And there are photographs that were taken in 1992 as well, when Mr. Praljak went to Mostar. I'll show you the photograph.

utterances.speaker: MR. PORYVAEV
utterances.text: Your Honour, I have no further questions. Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. It's now 20 to 4.00. We will have a 20-minute break, and we will resume at 4.00 p.m. Defence counsel will have two hours at its disposal, and we will make sure that additional time is not used. Thank you, and we will resume in 20 minutes' time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [No interpretation]

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Can you hear the English? Can you hear?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Let me repeat. Witness, you're going to be answering questions put to you by the Defence counsel and perhaps also by the accused. Remain calm because sometimes the questions can be very direct and might upset you, but do your best to keep calm and to answer as precisely as possible and strictly within the frameworks of the question. Don't broach other areas which might be of great interest to you but is of relative interest to us. So stick to the question. And the cross-examination has the right to ask you this type of question in a very direct manner. I'm sure you'll be able to answer. I think, Mr. Karnavas, you want to start off, do you?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Well, Mr. President, on behalf of all of the Defence, we'd like to thank the gentleman for coming here. We don't believe that any cross-examination would, with this particular witness, advance our quest for the truth, so therefore we don't have any cross-examination, but I believe that Mr. Ibrisimovic does have two questions or two points of clarification. But one other point. The gentleman did indicate that he had some photographs taken with General Praljak. We understand that he has them with him. If it would be possible for the gentleman to turn them over or at least maybe copies for us or for the registry to make copies of those photographs, I think that would be something that we would welcome. But in any event, we wish to thank the gentleman for coming here, and again we don't believe that any cross-examination would advance our quest for the truth in light of his testimony on direct examination.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Sir, you have heard what the Defence has said. You said you had photographs on you, with you. So the Defence would like to see them. Could you hand them over to us so that we can make photocopies of them and then you can take the originals home. Do you have the photographs with you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I do, Your Honour, yes. Your Honour, I'll give you the first photograph for you to photocopy and to see who Mr. Praljak was sitting with, and then later on I'll give you the second photograph to have a look at or, rather, to photocopy. Here's one and here's the other.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: If we could put it up on the ELMO, Your Honour, just so we can have a -- I'm getting assistance from my colleagues.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. We're going to put them on the overhead projector, quite right, so that everyone can see them. I just wanted to show Mr. Praljak the photograph, but thanks to the ELMO we can see it. And where was the photo taken? Where are you there? Or who are you? Which one is you in the photograph, the one up front? The one up front.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. It was an honour for me at the time to have my photograph taken with Mr. Praljak. The first photograph is Mr. Praljak, Mr. Arif Pasalic, Kiho Nasis [phoen], Kemal Pilot, and Hasic. He's also a pilot and now has a chemist's in the town of Mostar, is the proprietor of a chemist. I don't think photographs lie, that this photograph can lie. It shows us together.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And what about the second photograph? There are five people there too. Who's on the second photograph?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] On the second photograph the same people I was with, Mr. Praljak, Arif Pasalic, Ica Lasic, Hasic the pilot, and Kemo the pilot. Now, this young man, Kemo, is working, and Hasic is the proprietor of a chemist shop in Mostar, a pharmacy.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] On the first photograph there are six of you. So one person took the photograph. Who was the seventh? Who took the photograph. The seventh person who took the photograph, who was that? Unless it was one of those automatic cameras that take photographs when positioned themselves.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No. The first time I took the photograph with Mr. Praljak, Pasalic, Ica Lasic, Kemo, and Hasic. And the second photograph is the one that I wanted to be in, too, with the gentlemen, and that photograph was taken by Mr. Sisirak, Hara took the photograph. It's a cafe in the old town right by the Old Bridge.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Praljak, yes, you have the floor.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good afternoon, sir.

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA HADROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: Just a small question. Was this it taken in April 1993? I'm sure you'll remember -- as far as I remember it, this was April 1993, mid-April somewhere.

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA HADROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Thereabouts, yes, because the conflicts hadn't started yet. We had crossed the Neretva and went back from Podvelezje and from Velez. We returned from there. Mr. Praljak, you know that we all came back from Podvelezje and that the Chetniks had left at the time and had gone to Nevesinje.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: But if you remember correctly, and I'm sure you remember correctly because I also remember this, this photograph, as far as I remember, was taken roughly in mid-April 1993.

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA HADROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Before the conflicts. Just prior to the conflicts.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: Yes, prior to the conflicts. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Registrar, can the usher go and make a photocopy of the originals and then we can give the originals back and have an IC number. Mr. Ibrisimovic, I think you have some questions to ask.

utterances.speaker: MR. IBRISIMOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, my question is just by way of clarification and what was in the transcript.

utterances.speaker: MR. IBRISIMOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We saw a document?

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Slowly, please, numbers.

utterances.speaker: MR. IBRISIMOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation].

utterances.speaker: MR. IBRISIMOVIC
utterances.text: The exchange document dated the 15th, 1993. P 05077. I'd just like to clarify one point. It's on page 9 of the transcript. The witness said that the Red Cross registered their names for the first time on the 16th or 18th of August. It doesn't matter. 1993. It's not important. But is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA HADROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. IBRISIMOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That's all, Mr. President. I just wanted to have that in the transcript, because I don't think it was clearly recorded. I have no further questions. I thank the witness for coming to testify.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I apologise. May I say that I have the document of when we left and the number under which I left, the number I was recorded by the Red Cross.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, thank you. Mr. Poryvaev, no re-examination, I don't expect, because there were no questions from the Defence teams or just confirmation of the photograph?

utterances.speaker: MR. PORYVAEV
utterances.text: No, Your Honour, I have no examination.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Registrar, may we give IC numbers for the two photographs, please.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President. The photograph with the witness will be given Exhibit number IC 443, and the second photograph without the witness will be given Exhibit number IC 444. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. On behalf of my colleagues, Witness, I thank you for having come to The Hague to testify about the events that took place in your own country. I would like to express best wishes for your safe return home. And as you're going to retire soon, we wish you a happy retirement. I'm now going to ask Madam Usher to escort you out of the courtroom and to return the two photographs to you as soon as possible. Thank you, Witness.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] May I be allowed to thank you, Your Honours, too. And I would just like to say or, rather, to change one thing that is something from my life. When I gave my statements, I mentioned there was a mistake in the writing of a name and a surname, because I don't want that my child tomorrow or the child of the accused say that I hurt him in any way, did evil to him, and I don't want that to happen. And I mentioned this a moment ago. I mentioned his first name and last name a moment ago. It was Berislav Pusic, and I can frankly say that this will remain with me for as long as I live, and I can thank him for being alive today. And I have every confidence in you, Your Honours, that you will make your rulings according to justice and that you know what I experienced and all the hardships I went through. Mr. Prlic knows full well. He worked with Cibo and I was a car mechanic for his car. He knows that in the Presidency at that time I had --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Sir, thank you. We have taken note of what you said about Mr. Pusic, and I'm now going to ask the usher to escort you out of the courtroom.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I turn to the Prosecution for the schedule for the coming days. There's a witness for the next few days. No protective measures for witnesses. There were no -- for the next four days, a witness for the next four days. There are no protective measures that have been requested. Seven hours have been envisaged for the examination-in-chief of this next witness, which will probably take us two days, and then I think the cross-examination can start on Tuesday and go on into Wednesday and Thursday. So that is the schedule for the end of February and the beginning of March. And in March we also have a programme with another witness who will be coming in for the next four days after the first four days. Is that right, Mr. Scott?

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honours. Good afternoon. That's correct. We expect the witnesses for the next two weeks to be very substantial witnesses and also involve a fair amount of -- well, a substantial amount of documentation, and we do think that allowing for both the direct examination and the cross-examinations, they will both take the better part of a four-day trial week.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. I would like to inform the Prosecution and counsel that I am going to be the Judge in Mr. Seselj's trial -- the Pre-Trial Judge for the Seselj trial, so I will have to sit in two proceedings. If there are no other matters, we're going to adjourn. Mr. Karnavas.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President. I noticed today as I walked into court and I turned on the monitor that on the Tribunet there was a short indication, a short advertisement, as -- you could put it that way, that in the Gotovina case the Trial Chamber ordered the Prosecution to reduce the indictment. I mention that because I think that -- that we've made this request on several occasions. We know that there's a -- at least a -- based on the Appeals Chamber's decision the matter was remanded back for further review or explanations, but again we would call upon the Trial Chamber to revisit that issue and perhaps issue an order to the Prosecutor to reduce the indictment or perhaps we could have a 65 ter meeting in open session to see how we can reduce the indictment. I think it's fair if others are doing it. This was done by Judge Bonomy in his case. It's being done in the Gotovina case. The Rules have been changed, and in light of the time schedules and time pressures, I think this is something that perhaps the Trial Chamber may wish to revisit. I throw it out there for your consideration.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'll give you the floor, Mr. Scott, but I'd just like to say something before that. As you know, we had Article 73 bis and paragraph (D) that states that, "after having heard the Prosecution the Chamber of the first instance in order to guarantee a rapid trial invites the Prosecutor to reduce the number of charges in the indictment," et cetera, et cetera. Now, when this text was adopted by the Plenary Assembly, the Prlic case was already under way, and at the Plenary meeting I asked my colleagues if there could be a ruling which would be retroactive on this particular Rule. I have not received a clear answer on the subject yet, so I am waiting for a reply about the modification of this Article. And the -- I asked for the text to be modified. I asked the Rules Committee to do that, because this Article seems to come under the competence of the Chamber before the trial, because it says "Pre-Trial Conference." So there's a problem there. If we did not have this problem, then quite obviously the Trial Chamber would have asked the Prosecution to react as you have suggested, but since the reading of the text as it stands now does not allow for this possibility once the trial is under way, we can't budge on that point. Of course, if the Defence really wish and consider that we are competent in doing that, then they can present arguments along those lines. I think myself that it would be possible, but I'm not quite certain. I can't be 100 per cent certain. That is why I contacted the Rules Committee, to be more precise about this matter. Now, Mr. Karnavas, what I have said and what Mr. Scott has said and will say -- well, I know that you attend all the work of the Rules Committee, so you probably have a vision. What is the Prosecution's position on the points raised by Mr. Karnavas?

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Well, on that last point -- excuse me. On the last point, Your Honour, the same might also note because I know the Chamber said this before on Mr. Karnavas's participation on the Rules Committee. I also am on the Rules Committee, have been on the Rules Committee for the past four years -- at least four years, I think, before Mr. Karnavas came on. So I also attend every Rules committee meeting, number one. Secondly, Your Honour, I don't think it's fruitful to debate what -- what might have been done at a previous time. There's a lot of Rules of course that have not been applied in this case. Among those is Rule 65 ter (F) which would require the Defence to state what is disputed and not disputed. That Rule has never been applied in this case either, unfortunately. So, Your Honour, we are where we are. The Prosecution would resist to be perfectly transparent any such order in this case at this time. This trial went through a -- case went through an extensive pre-trial process. The trial has now been going on for almost a year, and it is unfortunately in our view, or fortunately or unfortunately -- thank you, Judge Prandler -- too late to expect the Prosecution to substantially redesign its case. Most of the crime base has now been presented. We are finishing that up in the next few weeks, and we would -- we are not agreeable to counsel's suggestion. We agree with the Chamber's interpretation, it does not apply to this case, and in any event, it would be too late to apply the Rule now. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Anyway, as you know, the Chamber will be making a ruling, because we also received a motion on certain aspects of that question. So we will be making a ruling in due course, but obviously the Rule gives the Prosecution all the powers to modify the indictment, but there must be agreement from the Chamber. So you are the -- you are in control in this case. And we shall be rendering a decision in due course and responding to that. Mr. Kovacic.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, perhaps this isn't the right time for a debate, but I'd just like to say something with respect to the retroactive application of the said Rule. Of course, the Trial Chamber will find sources that it can use for interpretation, but I'd just like to indicate to the Trial Chamber that the national -- that according to national law in the former Yugoslavia, and also this applies to all the republics after Yugoslavia, had the material -- a material legal provision in criminal cases when it -- we are dealing with material law in fact meant that if a law is modified and amended after the trial has gone into process then the mitigating circumstance is allowed. And also, the -- it was up to the Court to apply the Rules that are more favourable to the accused if there was an amendment when the trial was already under way. We all agree that according to the practice in this court and the source of law that this particular law of the Yugoslav republics and the former Yugoslavia is one possible source and allows for interpretation. And that's what I wanted to say.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Your Honour, if I might have one more moment, and I think I might speak, perhaps rarely, for perhaps all the parties at this point. I know both the Prosecution and the Defence made a filing -- have made filings in the past couple of weeks and I say this in reference to Your Honour's comment a moment ago that you anticipate issuing a further ruling on the question of time. I think it's fair to say, as both all the parties have indicated, the parties would expect or anticipate being heard further prior to any ruling on that basis. We don't believe there's anything additional in the record now which would provide any further justification for the time cut that is in the current record. There is no justification for the original court order now is there any new information since the Appeals Chamber ruling that would justify the time that has been cut from the Prosecution case. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. We have taken note of what you have said, and there will be a ruling. I think that we took note of five or six decisions today -- registered five or six decisions, so we're working very quickly, and this ruling will probably be forthcoming within the space of next week. Having said that, we reconvene on Monday at 2.15. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: to be reconvened on Monday, the 26th day of February, 2007, at 2.15 p.m.

procedural_notes.text: --- Whereupon the hearing adjourned at 4.28 p.m.,
